strengths: The combination of a compact persistent workspace, competition among patches across a batch, and associative retrieval is a coherent architectural proposal with potential usefulness as a ViT extension.

Table 1 reports meaningful gains over the corresponding ViT baselines. AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, with parameters increasing from 14.9M to 15.8M. Gains also persist for the Base configuration.

The component ablations provide useful evidence. Removing the bottleneck reduces CIFAR-10 accuracy from 83.34% to 75.40%, while replacing Hopfield retrieval with cross-attention reduces it to 81.03%. Figure 4 also demonstrates favorable accuracy–parameter tradeoffs relative to Coordination.

The manuscript includes memory-initialization and temperature studies, attention visualizations, and multiple classification and reasoning datasets. It appropriately acknowledges its weaker performance on relational questions.
weaknesses: The central retrieval operation is insufficiently specified, and its distinction from attention is overstated. For projected memories P, the standard continuous Hopfield update is q_new = P^T softmax(beta Pq), an attention operation with tied keys and values. Equation 8 instead specifies an unqualified argmin without an initialization, update algorithm, iteration count, stopping criterion, or differentiation procedure. These details determine the implemented method and its computational cost; the energy expression alone does not establish the claimed fundamental difference from attention.

The complexity claims are unsupported as stated. Computing the attention matrix requires scoring all M memory slots against all BN patches before top-k selection; masking afterward does not eliminate this cost. The architecture also retains ordinary per-image self-attention. Section 4.1 compares against O((BN)^2), although the ViT baseline attends separately within each image. Fixed memory capacity therefore does not establish complexity invariance to input quantity or dimension. Parameter counts provide evidence of compactness in some configurations, but no runtime, FLOP, or peak-memory measurements establish the broader efficiency claims.

The proposed balance loss has a technical ambiguity affecting its claimed mechanism. In Equation 5, A was defined as dense softmax attention, making every load count equal to M. If top-k-masked attention is intended, the hard selection counts have zero gradient almost everywhere, and no estimator or relaxation is described. The importance term can still supply gradients, but the load term's optimization role is unexplained. Figures 8–9 show diversity increasing during training without a loss-disabled control, and Table 2 omits a balance-loss ablation, so its causal contribution remains unestablished.

The evaluation protocol for persistent, batch-dependent memory is missing. The paper does not specify whether memory is frozen or updated during testing, how it is initialized between evaluation passes, or whether test updates carry into subsequent training. Because predictions can depend on other images and prior batches, these choices materially affect interpretation and reproducibility. No batch-composition, batch-size, or per-image-workspace control isolates the proposed benefit of pooling patches across examples.

The evidence supports classification improvements more clearly than improved relational association or specialized modules. On relational Sort-of-CLEVR questions, AiT achieves 67.74%, below Coordination's 73.43% and CNN+RN's 81.07%. Spatially different attention maps demonstrate differing responses but do not establish stable semantic specialization. The main accuracy tables also omit variability despite reporting three-run means, limiting assessment of smaller differences.

A readily correctable reporting inconsistency further impedes reproduction: Section 5.1 specifies an initial learning rate of 1e-5, whereas Table 6 lists 1e-4. The grid-search ranges and validation protocol are also unspecified. The worthwhile classification gains are outweighed primarily by the unresolved retrieval, loss, complexity, and evaluation issues above.

strengths: Combining a shared low-dimensional memory, sparse writing, and associative retrieval provides a coherent, potentially useful extension to ViT. Competition among patches from different images is an interesting architectural feature.

Table 1 reports consistent CIFAR improvements over comparable ViT configurations. AiT-Small achieves 83.34% versus 79.53% on CIFAR-10 and 56.30% versus 53.19% on CIFAR-100, with parameters increasing from 14.9M to 15.8M. Improvements also persist in the Base configuration.

Table 2 provides meaningful component evidence: removing the bottleneck reduces CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 accuracy to 75.40%/46.53%, while replacing Hopfield retrieval with cross-attention yields 81.03%/54.96%. These results support the practical value of the proposed combination.

The evaluation includes classification, geometric reasoning, and visual question answering. Memory initialization and temperature studies, attention visualizations, three-run averages, and detailed architectural settings provide useful characterization beyond headline accuracy.
weaknesses: The prediction protocol is insufficiently specified for an architecture that mixes examples and maintains memory. Section 4.1 pools patches across a batch, and the reset-memory ablation implies persistence across training batches, but test-time memory initialization, updating, and resetting are not explained. Batch-size/order sensitivity and a per-image workspace control are absent. Consequently, the evaluated prediction function and conditions under which the gains hold remain unclear; this is a consequential reproducibility concern.

The load component of the proposed balance loss is ineffective as written. Section 4.2 defines A as softmax attention, so every entry is positive and Equation 5 assigns the same load M to every position, making its variance zero. If masked attention is intended, the hard indicator has zero gradient almost everywhere, with no gradient estimator specified. The importance term can still supply gradients, but the claimed two-component mechanism lacks adequate technical justification. Figures 8–9 show changes during training without a comparison excluding this loss.

Hopfield retrieval is underspecified, and its distinction from attention is overstated. Equation 8 gives an argmin without an update rule, iteration count, stopping criterion, or differentiation procedure. A global minimizer does not preserve dependence on the starting patch; input-initialized local retrieval needs to be defined. Moreover, for H = f_LT(gamma), the standard energy yields the fixed-point equation xi = H^T softmax(beta H xi), a tied-key/value attention operation. This narrows the supported novelty to the architectural integration and weakens the claim of a fundamentally different retrieval mechanism.

The complexity claims conflate fixed memory capacity with computational cost. Before top-k selection, the method constructs an M-by-(B*N) attention matrix, requiring O(M*B*N*D) scoring work per head. Input projections and retrieval also depend on embedding dimensions, and the full architecture retains quadratic within-image self-attention. Thus, input-size/dimension invariance and the stated O(B*N*k) explanation are not established. Parameter-count comparisons alone do not demonstrate runtime or activation-memory advantages.

The evidence supports narrower claims than general superiority in association and reasoning. On relational Sort-of-CLEVR, AiT reaches 67.74%, below Coordination at 73.43% and CNN+RN at 81.07%. The principal comparison tables omit dispersion despite reporting three-run means, limiting assessment of smaller gains. A separate, readily correctable reproducibility issue is the learning-rate discrepancy between Section 5.1 (1e-5) and Table 6 (1e-4). The rejection direction is driven primarily by the unresolved mechanism and evaluation issues above, rather than benchmark breadth or this presentation discrepancy.

strengths: The combination of batch-wide patch competition, compact persistent memory, and associative retrieval is an interesting architectural contribution with potential usefulness as a ViT extension.

Table 1 provides meaningful comparisons against the same ViT backbone. AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 accuracy from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, with parameters increasing from 14.9M to 15.8M. Improvements also hold for the Base variant. These gains have value independently of benchmark-leading performance.

Table 2 contains useful component ablations. Removing the bottleneck reduces CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 accuracy to 75.40%/46.53%, while replacing Hopfield retrieval with cross-attention yields 81.03%/54.96%. Memory initialization and temperature studies provide additional evidence about the method's behavior.
weaknesses: The memory evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified. Sections 4.1–4.2 mix patches across samples and maintain memory through moving-average updates, but the manuscript does not explain whether memory is frozen, updated, or reset during testing and between training and evaluation. Predictions could consequently depend on batch composition and previous batches. Without this specification or controls for batch size and per-image processing, the reported gains are difficult to interpret and reproduce. This is a deciding concern.

The load component of the proposed balance loss lacks a useful gradient as written. Equation (5) counts positive entries of A, previously defined as softmax attention; these entries are positive, making every load equal to M and its variance zero. If masked attention is intended instead, the hard counts are piecewise constant and supply no ordinary gradient. No surrogate is described. The importance component can still train, but Figures 8–9 show changes over training without a loss-disabled control, leaving the claimed contribution of this loss unresolved.

Hopfield retrieval is both underspecified and overstated as fundamentally different from attention. Equations (7)–(8) provide an energy and an argmin without an executable update procedure, iteration count, or differentiation strategy. For stored patterns X, the standard fixed-point update is Xᵀ softmax(βXξ), an attention operation with tied keys and values. The architectural combination can still be useful, but the manuscript does not adequately establish what its retrieval contributes beyond this known connection.

The efficiency claims exceed the analysis and measurements. The bottleneck still requires constructing scores between M slots and BN patches before top-k selection; projection and retrieval costs also remain, and AiT retains ordinary within-image self-attention. Fixed memory capacity therefore does not establish complexity invariant to input quantity or dimension. Parameter counts alone do not substantiate computational or runtime savings, and no throughput or peak-memory measurements are reported.

The evidence supports classification improvements more clearly than general reasoning or functional specialization. On relational Sort-of-CLEVR, AiT reaches 67.74%, below Coordination at 73.43% and CNN+RN at 81.07%. Spatial attention maps and increasing patch diversity do not independently demonstrate distinct functional specializations. The main tables also omit variability despite reporting three-run averages. These limitations narrow the supported claims; limited benchmark breadth alone is not the reason for rejection.

A smaller reproducibility issue is the conflicting learning rate: Section 5.1 states 1e-5, whereas Table 6 states 1e-4. This is readily correctable, but the unresolved algorithm, evaluation, and efficiency concerns above outweigh the worthwhile empirical gains and determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: AiT offers a worthwhile architectural combination: a compact persistent workspace, sparse top-k writes across image patches, and associative retrieval integrated into a ViT. This provides a plausible mechanism for sharing information across samples.

The strongest evidence is the improvement over corresponding ViT backbones in Table 1. AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, adding only 0.9M parameters. Improvements also appear for the Base configuration.

The evaluation includes multiple classification datasets and relational reasoning, reports means over three runs, and examines initialization and inverse temperature. Attention visualizations and energy measurements help explain the model's behavior, and the manuscript acknowledges its weaker relational-reasoning result.
weaknesses: The central complexity claim is unsupported by the specified computation. Section 4.2 constructs dense scores between M memory slots and BN patches before applying top-k, requiring work proportional to MBN and the feature dimension. Retrieval and input projections also scale with input size, while AiT retains ordinary quadratic self-attention within each image. Fixed workspace capacity therefore does not establish the claimed invariance to input quantities and dimensions. Parameter-count comparisons alone, without runtime, FLOPs, or peak-memory measurements, do not substantiate computational efficiency.

The retrieval operation is insufficiently specified, and its distinction from attention is overstated. Equations (7)–(8) provide an energy and an argmin without an executable update rule, iteration count, stopping criterion, or differentiation procedure. A global argmin also does not specify the input-dependent local retrieval described in the text. For stored patterns P, the standard continuous-Hopfield update is Pᵀsoftmax(βPξ), which is attention with shared keys and values. Consequently, the claim of a fundamentally different retrieval mechanism and the interpretation of the W/O Hopfield ablation require a more precise account.

The proposed balance loss has a substantive mathematical ambiguity. In Equation (5), A was defined as softmax attention, so every entry is positive and the load count is constant. If A instead means the masked top-k attention, the hard indicator has zero gradient almost everywhere; no surrogate estimator is specified. The importance term can still provide gradients, but the claimed contribution of load balancing is unestablished. Figures 8–9 show changes during training without a loss-disabled control, and Table 2 does not ablate this loss. Increased patch coverage alone also provides limited evidence for stable, distinct specialization.

The cross-batch memory makes the evaluation protocol consequential, yet it is not described adequately. The squash layer mixes samples, and Equation (4) maintains evolving state, but the manuscript does not specify whether memory is frozen, updated, or reset during testing, or how gradients and state are handled between training batches. Predictions may depend on batch composition and evaluation order. No batch-size sensitivity study or per-image workspace control establishes how much of the gain comes from cross-sample information sharing or how the model behaves for individual-image inference.

The evidence supports a narrower benefit than the broad superiority claims. On relational Sort-of-CLEVR, AiT achieves 67.74%, below Coordination's 73.43% and CNN+RN's 81.07%; Triangle performance does not improve over ViT. Oxford Pet is presented mainly through a learning-curve plot. Although three-run means are reported, the main comparison tables omit dispersion, limiting assessment of smaller differences. These limitations constrain the demonstrated usefulness beyond the consistent CIFAR gains.

Additional reporting issues are secondary but affect reproducibility and clarity. Section 5.1 gives an initial learning rate of 1e-5, while Table 6 lists 1e-4 without explaining their relationship; grid-search ranges and the validation/model-selection protocol are unspecified. strengths: The combination of persistent low-dimensional memory, sparse workspace writing, and Hopfield-style retrieval is a coherent, potentially useful augmentation to vision Transformers.

Table 1 demonstrates consistent CIFAR improvements: AiT-Small achieves 83.34/56.30% on CIFAR-10/100 versus ViT-Small's 79.53/53.19%, with 15.8M versus 14.9M parameters. AiT-Medium also exceeds ViT-Base on both datasets using substantially fewer parameters.

The component ablations provide meaningful evidence for the architecture. Removing the bottleneck reduces CIFAR-10 accuracy from 83.34% to 75.40%. Evaluation extends to relational reasoning, where AiT improves over Coordination from 73.43% to 76.82%, although CNN+RN remains stronger.

Appendix A.5 usefully specifies the test-time memory protocol and evaluates disabling memory-forward computation. The nearly unchanged CIFAR results support the usefulness of the stored training memory independently of current-batch adaptation.
weaknesses: The claimed fundamental distinction between associative retrieval and attention is not technically supported. For stored patterns S, the standard update associated with Eq. (7) is S^T softmax(beta S x), which is attention with shared keys and values. Replacing this with learned multi-head attention also changes parameterization, so the ablation does not isolate a fundamentally different retrieval principle. Furthermore, the stated single-step implementation does not establish the exact minimization in Eq. (8) or the convergence claims in Appendix A.7. These issues materially weaken the novelty and mechanistic justification.

The proposed balance loss has an unresolved optimization issue. If A in Eq. (5) denotes the previously defined softmax scores, every entry is positive and every load count equals M, making its variance zero. If A instead denotes top-k-masked scores, the Boolean load counts have zero gradient almost everywhere; no gradient estimator is specified. The importance term can still train, but the claimed contribution of the load term is unsupported. Figures 9–10 show progression during training without a loss-on/off control establishing the loss's effect.

The computational-efficiency claims exceed the evidence. Section 4.2 computes all M × BN attention scores before top-k selection, and every AiT block retains dense per-image self-attention. Fixed memory capacity therefore does not establish computation independent of input quantity or dimension, or eliminate quadratic self-attention cost. Parameter counts alone cannot substantiate runtime or activation-memory advantages; FLOPs, throughput, and peak-memory measurements are absent.

Several comparisons do not isolate the claimed benefits adequately. The parameter-efficiency comparison against ViT-Base lacks a corresponding ViT-Medium baseline, and the relational-reasoning comparison omits plain ViT despite AiT retaining self-attention. Means over three runs are reported without variability in the main tables, limiting interpretation of smaller differences.

Standard inference remains dependent on which test samples share a batch: the persistent memory is frozen, but temporary memory used for retrieval incorporates the current batch. Batch-size and batch-composition sensitivity are not evaluated. The without-memory-forward results mitigate this concern, particularly on CIFAR, but do not establish robustness of the standard protocol.

Secondary reproducibility issues include conflicting learning rates—1e-5 in Section 5.1 versus 1e-4 in Table 6—and unspecified handling of gradients through memory carried between training batches. The promised code is unavailable in the supplied manuscript. These are more readily correctable than the central concerns about the retrieval mechanism, balance loss, and efficiency claims that determine my weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: AiT offers a coherent integration of persistent low-dimensional memory, sparse patch selection, and associative retrieval into a ViT block. Sharing a compact workspace across training batches is a potentially useful architectural direction.

Matched-backbone comparisons support an empirical benefit. In Table 1, AiT-Small achieves 83.34%/56.30% on CIFAR-10/100 versus 79.53%/53.19% for ViT-Small, with 15.8M versus 14.9M parameters. Improvements also persist at Base scale.

The component ablations provide useful evidence for the overall design. Removing the bottleneck reduces CIFAR-10 accuracy from 83.34% to 75.40%, while replacing Hopfield retrieval with MHA gives 81.03% (Table 2). Initialization and temperature studies further characterize the method.

Evaluation extends beyond classification: AiT improves relational accuracy over Coordination from 73.43% to 76.82% on Sort-of-CLEVR. The appendix also explicitly describes frozen-memory evaluation and provides a useful control that disables memory forwarding.
weaknesses: The central balance-loss contribution is not technically established as written. Equation 5 counts positive entries of A, but A is defined as a softmax matrix, making every load equal to M and its variance zero. If the intended A is instead top-k-masked, the discrete count has no useful ordinary gradient; no relaxation or gradient estimator is specified. Moreover, Figures 9–10 show changes during training without a loss-disabled control, so they do not isolate whether this loss causes specialization or improves accuracy.

The Hopfield-specific contribution is overstated. With P denoting the projected memory, the standard update associated with Equation 7 is P^T softmax(beta P xi), which is attention over memory with tied keys and values. This does not support the claimed fundamental distinction from attention. Replacing it with fully parameterized MHA changes the projection structure as well as the proposed mechanism. Separately, Equation 8's argmin and Appendix A.7's claim that all patches reach their minimum are not justified by the single update normally used; energy reduction does not establish convergence.

The computational-efficiency claims are inadequately supported. The method computes the full M-by-(B N) attention-score matrix before top-k selection, while ordinary per-image self-attention remains in every block. A fixed number of selected patches therefore does not make computation independent of input quantity or dimension. Low-dimensional memory can reduce storage and projection costs, but parameter counts alone do not establish the claimed computational savings; runtime, FLOPs, peak memory, and input-scaling measurements are absent.

The distinctive role of communication across samples and time remains insufficiently isolated. Inference still constructs memory from the current test batch, making predictions potentially dependent on batch composition, without a batch-size or composition sensitivity study. Table 7 is reassuring but shows only 0.09/0.02 percentage-point CIFAR-10/100 gains from memory forwarding. These results do not isolate the benefit of batch-wide competition over an otherwise matched per-image memory mechanism.

Experimental and reporting limitations weaken attribution of the gains. The parameter-efficiency comparison lacks ViT-Medium, and the relational evaluation omits a matched ViT baseline. Main tables report three-run means without dispersion, and the validation/grid-search protocol is unspecified. As a secondary reproducibility clarification, the relationship between the initial learning rate of 1e-5 in Section 5.1 and the 1e-4 rate in Table 6 should be explained. The decisive reservations concern the unsupported mechanism and efficiency claims, despite the worthwhile controlled accuracy improvements.

strengths: The architecture offers a potentially useful combination of persistent low-dimensional memory, top-k patch selection, and associative retrieval. Using the same memory for attention queries and retrieval patterns gives the design a coherent structure.

The matched ViT comparisons show consistent benefits. In Table 1, AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 accuracy from 79.53/53.19 to 83.34/56.30 with a modest parameter increase. AiT-Medium also exceeds ViT-Base on both datasets using 45.9M versus 85.7M parameters.

For stored patterns P, the standard update associated with the cited energy is P^T softmax(beta P x), which is attention with shared keys and values. Thus the claim that retrieval fundamentally differs from attention is overstated. Equation 8 specifies an exact argmin, but the implementation reportedly uses one step; energy reduction does not generally establish minimization or convergence to a stored prior. Replacing this operation with full multi-head attention also changes projections and heads, so Table 2 does not isolate a benefit from associative dynamics.

The proposed balance loss has an unresolved technical issue. As defined before Equation 5, A is a dense softmax, making every indicator A > 0 equal to one and the load-variance term zero. If post-top-k attention is intended, the hard selection count has zero derivative almost everywhere, and no gradient estimator is described. Furthermore, Figures 9–10 show changes during training without a loss-free control; they do not establish that this loss causes specialization or improves task accuracy.

The computational claims are not supported by the actual operations. Section 4.1 compares against O((BN)^2) attention across an entire batch, whereas conventional ViT performs separate attention within each image. AiT retains that dense self-attention and computes all memory-to-patch scores before top-k selection. Projection and retrieval costs also depend on input dimensions and memory size. Parameter counts alone do not demonstrate the claimed efficiency, and no runtime, FLOP, or peak-memory measurements are supplied.

The broader experimental conclusions are less secure than the matched ViT improvements. Table 1 includes substantially different model capacities, and unusually weak baseline results, such as Luna's 47.86% CIFAR-10 accuracy, are not investigated. Table 4 lacks a plain ViT control for attributing relational-reasoning improvements to the workspace. Main result tables report three-run means without dispersion. The experiments establish promise under the reported training settings, but provide limited evidence for the broader superiority claims.

Reproducibility and positioning have additional, secondary ambiguities: gradient handling through persistent EMA memory updates is unspecified; Section 5.1 and Table 6 give learning-rate values whose relationship is unclear; and the claim that previous latent-memory methods require equal input and latent dimensions conflicts with Table 5's characterization of Perceiver. These refinements alone would not determine rejection. The decisive concerns are the insufficiently established retrieval, balance-loss, and efficiency claims, which currently outweigh the worthwhile empirical improvements.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements over the corresponding ViT baseline: AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, adding only 0.9M parameters. AiT-Medium also exceeds ViT-Base on both CIFAR datasets with 45.9M versus 85.7M parameters.

weaknesses: The central retrieval formulation is insufficiently specified and its guarantees are overstated. Equation (8) defines an exact energy minimizer, whereas Section 3.4 implements only one unspecified update and claims that all patches reach their minima. A standard Hopfield update can decrease energy without reaching a minimum, and stored patterns are not automatically fixed-point attractors. Appendix F's energy plots do not establish these stronger claims.

The distinct contribution of Hopfield retrieval over attention is not adequately isolated. Equation (7) uses the standard modern-Hopfield energy, whose usual update is a softmax attention readout over stored patterns. The replacement ablation introduces separately parameterized multi-head cross-attention and changes computation substantially (Table 3). It therefore supports the chosen implementation but does not establish a distinct associative mechanism beyond attention.

The proposed load-balancing term has a technical problem as written. Equation (5) counts positive entries of A, which was defined as a softmax matrix; these counts are consequently constant. If A instead denotes masked top-k scores, the indicator is nondifferentiable, and no gradient estimator is specified. Figures 7–8 show diversity increasing during training without a corresponding loss-disabled control, leaving the claimed causal benefit of this term unsupported.

The comparisons do not establish the headline claims. Table 5 omits the original Relation Network associated with Santoro et al. (2017), so outperforming the listed baselines does not substantiate a new Sort-of-CLEVR state of the art. It also lacks a plain ViT control to isolate the memory contribution to reasoning. Similarly, the principal parameter-efficiency comparison lacks a six-layer ViT baseline matching AiT-Medium.

The inference procedure is ambiguous in consequential ways. Section 4.1 says memory is frozen during evaluation, while Section 3.3 explains test batch-size robustness through continued memory updates. With test batch size one, CIFAR supplies only 64 patches against the specified top-k capacity of 512; the manuscript must distinguish disabled writing from an altered selection rule. The actual retrieval update and handling of gradients through persistent memory are also unspecified, limiting reproducibility.

Secondary limitations concern efficiency and reporting. AiT retains dense self-attention and computes attention scores before top-k selection, so sparse memory writing alone does not establish computational scalability. Table 3 measures retrieval overhead without broader runtime evidence. The learning rate differs between Section 4.1 and Table 7, and the main tables omit variability despite averaging three runs. These reporting issues are secondary; the unresolved mechanism, attribution, and evaluation concerns above determine the weak-reject recommendation.

weaknesses: The central retrieval operation is insufficiently specified, and its guarantees are overstated (Section 3.4, Equations 7–8). Equation 8 specifies exact energy minimization, but the implementation reportedly uses one iteration without giving its explicit update rule. Together with the unresolved core formulation, these missing controls determine my weak-reject recommendation despite the useful classification gains.

The novelty of the retrieval mechanism needs more precise separation from established Hopfield attention. Equation 7 uses the standard modern Hopfield energy, whose usual single-step retrieval corresponds to attention with tied keys and values. Replacing it with differently parameterized multi-head cross-attention does not isolate the benefit of the energy interpretation. The clearest contribution is the particular memory-and-bottleneck architecture.

Reproducibility is incomplete: Section 4.1 specifies a learning rate of 1e-5, whereas Table 7 gives 1e-4. Section 3.3 explains evaluation batch-size robustness through smoothed memory updates, whereas Section 4.1 states that memory is frozen during evaluation. Gradient handling through persistent memory and the validation protocol for grid search are not specified. The main tables report means without variability estimates.

Efficiency evidence supports a parameter/depth tradeoff, while practical scalability remains uncertain. AiT retains dense self-attention in every block, and Table 3 isolates retrieval overhead rather than comparing complete models' runtime or peak memory. Table 1 supports meaningful gains under the reported training setup. AiT-Small achieves 83.34%/56.30% on CIFAR-10/100 versus ViT-Small’s 79.53%/53.19%, using 15.8M versus 14.9M parameters. AiT-Medium also exceeds ViT-Base on both datasets with 45.9M versus 85.7M parameters.

The Hopfield retrieval procedure and its guarantees are insufficiently justified. Equation 8 specifies an exact minimizer, whereas Section 3.4 uses one iteration without giving the actual update. The missing six-layer ViT control also limits attribution of AiT-Medium’s advantage over twelve-layer ViT-Base to the memory mechanism rather than depth-dependent behavior.

Reproducibility is limited by unspecified gradient handling through memory updates across batches and an unclear validation protocol for the grid search. Secondary reporting issues include unreconciled learning-rate values in Section 4.1 and Table 7, and missing variability estimates in the main result tables. The worthwhile empirical gains keep this from a clear rejection, but the unresolved core learning mechanism, overstated retrieval guarantees, and insufficient support for headline claims currently tip the balance toward weak rejection.

Table 1 demonstrates meaningful gains under the reported training protocol. AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 accuracy from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, using 15.8M rather than 14.9M parameters. Figure 9 demonstrates energy reduction, but does not establish the stronger convergence claims. This affects reproducibility and the technical interpretation of the proposed mechanism.

The balance loss has a substantive optimization problem as written. Equation 5 counts positive attention entries, but the attention matrix defined in Section 3.2 is a softmax, making every load equal to the number of memory slots. If the intended matrix is instead masked by top-k selection, the hard indicator supplies no ordinary gradient for changing these counts; no surrogate or gradient estimator is specified. Moreover, Figures 7–8 compare different training epochs without a control that removes the balance loss, and Table 2 does not ablate this loss. Table 5 omits the Relation Network introduced by the cited Santoro et al. paper, as well as a plain ViT with the same backbone. The reported improvement over Coordination is valuable, but the attribution to associative memory remains insufficiently controlled.

Several reporting gaps reduce confidence in reproducibility and comparison reliability. Section 4.1 gives an initial learning rate of 1e-5, while Table 7 lists 1e-4 without reconciling them. The validation protocol for grid search and the Sort-of-CLEVR train/test partition are unspecified. The principal tables report three-run means without variability estimates, making smaller differences difficult to assess. These are secondary concerns, but they matter because code availability is only promised.

The demonstrated contribution is principally an integration of established memory, sparse attention, and modern-Hopfield ideas, with encouraging results in small-data settings. Broader usefulness remains uncertain, particularly given the roughly 20–30% Oxford Pet accuracies in Figure 2. strengths: The combination of low-dimensional explicit memory, sparse memory writing, and associative retrieval is coherent and potentially useful. Figure 1 explains the modular architecture clearly, and each workspace layer adds approximately 0.45M parameters.

The reported improvements over corresponding ViT baselines are consistent. In Table 1, AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 accuracy from 79.53/53.19% to 83.34/56.30%. AiT-Medium also exceeds ViT-Base on these datasets and ImageNet100 with 45.9M versus 85.7M parameters.

weaknesses: The selected-instance component of the proposed balance loss is ineffective as specified. Equation 3 uses the softmax attention matrix, whose entries are positive, making every load equal to M and its variance zero. If post-top-k attention is intended instead, the hard selection count has no useful gradient without an estimator, which is not described. The aggregate loss ablation does not establish the effectiveness of the advertised two-part objective.

The inference procedure is materially ambiguous. Section 3.2 says explicit memory is frozen during evaluation, whereas Appendix F reports benefits from retaining the cross-attention whose stated role is memory updating. The manuscript does not distinguish temporary updates from persistent updates or specify evaluation reset policies. Because writing pools tokens across samples, these choices determine whether predictions depend on other test examples and batch ordering.

The distinctive benefit of Hopfield retrieval is insufficiently isolated. A standard single-step modern-Hopfield update is softmax attention with tied keys and values. Replacing it with learned multi-head cross-attention changes parameterization and computational cost, so the ablation does not isolate an advantage from associative dynamics. Furthermore, one energy-decreasing step does not generally compute Equation 6's argmin or justify the assertion that all tokens reach their minima simultaneously.

The broader performance claims rely on baselines whose optimization adequacy is insufficiently established. Results include 34.62% for ViT-Base on ImageNet100 and 47.86% for Luna on CIFAR-10. Although author-recommended settings are claimed, the manuscript provides insufficient baseline tuning and convergence evidence to establish that these comparisons represent competitive implementations. This limits the generality of the measured gains.

The demonstrated efficiency advantage is primarily a reduction in required ViT depth. AiT retains dense self-attention and computes the full memory-to-token score matrix before top-k selection. Table 1 also shows AiT-Small using substantially more parameters and FLOPs than standard Coordination. Without runtime, peak-memory, or input-size scaling measurements, a general computational advantage over sparse Transformers remains unestablished.

Additional reproducibility gaps include the learning-rate discrepancy between Section 4.1 (1e-5) and Table 8 (1e-4), an unspecified ImageNet100 class subset, missing Sort-of-CLEVR split details, and unspecified gradient handling through persistent EMA memory. Some are readily correctable reporting issues; the central loss and inference ambiguities, together with insufficient isolation of the claimed retrieval contribution, determine the weak-reject recommendation.

The relational-reasoning improvements are substantial: Table 6 reports 80.03% for AiT-Base versus 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base. Evaluation across classification and relational tasks gives the architectural idea broader support than a single benchmark would.

The attention visualizations provide additional qualitative evidence of prior specialization.

Reproducibility also suffers from conflicting learning rates—1e-5 in Section 4.1 versus 1e-4 in Table 8—and missing details about validation-based hyperparameter selection and the ImageNet100 class subset. These reporting issues are secondary. The component ablations provide meaningful evidence beyond aggregate performance. Removing the bottleneck reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 56.30% to 46.53%; removing the balance loss reduces it to 54.72%. The memory visualizations, initialization experiments, and temperature sweep provide additional insight into model behavior.
weaknesses: The proposed load-balancing loss has a substantive mathematical problem. In Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1, A is defined by softmax, so every entry is positive and the selected-instance count in Equation 3 is identically M; its variance is therefore zero. Consequently, this component cannot provide the claimed training signal as written. Ablating the combined loss does not establish that both components work.

The evaluation-time memory behavior is unclear. Section 3.2 states that explicit memory is frozen during evaluation, but Appendix F reports an effect from retaining the bottleneck cross-attention, whose described function is to update that memory. The manuscript does not explain whether test-time writes are temporary or persistent. Because tokens are pooled across images, this distinction determines whether predictions depend on test-batch composition or ordering and materially affects reproducibility.

The Hopfield formulation and its claimed mechanism are insufficiently established. Equation 6 and Algorithm 1 specify an argmin instead of the implemented single-step update; an energy-decreasing step does not generally guarantee the stated simultaneous convergence to minima. Moreover, the standard one-step modern Hopfield update is cross-attention with tied keys and values. The replacement ablation uses full multi-head attention and changes computation substantially (Table 4), so it does not isolate a benefit attributable specifically to associative dynamics rather than parameterization.

The broad performance claims exceed the demonstrated experimental regime. ImageNet100 accuracy peaks at 36.72%, Oxford Pet accuracy is approximately 30%, and some reimplemented baselines perform poorly, such as Luna’s 47.86% on CIFAR-10. Although author-recommended settings are mentioned, detailed baseline configurations and tuning evidence are insufficient to assess these comparisons. The relative improvements remain valuable, but stronger evidence is needed to establish general superiority over competitive sparse architectures.

Efficiency evidence primarily supports reducing model depth. At matched depth, AiT adds parameters and FLOPs, retains dense self-attention, and computes attention scores before top-k selection. No wall-clock or peak-memory measurements establish the practical training-cost benefit of the batch-wide workspace.

Reproducibility is further limited by the unspecified ImageNet100 class subset, Sort-of-CLEVR train/test split, and validation protocol for grid search. The conflicting learning rates in Section 4.1 and Table 8 are a smaller reporting issue. Overall, the supported empirical gains are worthwhile, but the unresolved loss definition, inference protocol, and attribution of the central mechanism currently favor weak rejection.

Figure 1 clearly communicates the design.

The comparisons support improved accuracy with fewer ViT layers. AiT-Medium achieves 60.58% on CIFAR-100 versus ViT-Base's 57.92%, using 45.9M versus 85.7M parameters and 2.89 versus 5.60 billion reported FLOPs (Table 1). CIFAR-10 accuracy falls from 83.34% to 75.40% without the bottleneck, 81.03% when replacing Hopfield retrieval with cross-attention, and 81.89% without the balancing loss (Table 3). Reporting three-run means and variation for the principal classification comparisons strengthens this evidence.

In Equations 3–4, A is defined using softmax, so every entry is positive and the selected-instance count is identically M, giving zero load variance. The importance term remains trainable, but the claimed contribution of the load term is unsupported as written.

Table 9 usefully shows that most gains survive without test-time attention, but does not resolve the main evaluation protocol.

The Hopfield interpretation exceeds the demonstrated guarantee. For fixed memory P, the standard continuous-Hopfield update is P^T softmax(beta P x), equivalent to attention with tied keys and values. One update can reduce energy without solving the argmin in Equation 6 or reaching an attractor, as claimed in Section 3.4 and Algorithm 1. Figure 9 establishes energy reduction, not convergence. Moreover, replacing this operation with more parameterized multi-head attention does not isolate a benefit uniquely attributable to attractor dynamics. The integration remains interesting, but the retrieval novelty and explanation need narrower claims.

The efficiency evidence principally establishes reduced-depth gains relative to ViT. AiT retains dense self-attention and computes memory-to-token scores before top-k selection; no throughput, peak-memory, or sequence-length scaling measurements establish broader practical savings. Table 3 supports contributions from the bottleneck, balancing loss, and retrieval design. The supplementary visualizations and temperature analysis provide additional insight into model behavior.
weaknesses: The selected-instance component of the proposed balancing loss has a material technical problem. In Equation 3, the count sums indicators of positive attention scores. For the defined softmax attention, every score is positive, making this count constant and its variance zero. If the intended scores are masked after top-k selection, the hard count instead has zero gradient almost everywhere. No differentiable estimator is specified. The importance component can still contribute, but the claimed learning role of the selected-instance component is unsupported.

The retrieval formulation overstates what the implemented procedure establishes. Equation 6 and Algorithm 1 specify an argmin, while the implementation uses one update; energy reduction does not imply reaching a minimum or converging to a stored prior. The actual update is not explicitly given. With projected priors K, the standard modern Hopfield update is softmax(βXKᵀ)K, equivalent to attention with shared keys and values. The W/O Hopfield ablation replaces this with differently parameterized multihead attention, so it does not isolate a benefit specific to energy-based dynamics. The architectural integration may be useful, but the convergence and mechanistic claims exceed the evidence.

The memory lifecycle and evaluation protocol are insufficiently specified. Section 3.2 says memory is frozen during evaluation, whereas Appendix F shows that the memory-writing attention remains consequential at test time. The manuscript does not distinguish temporary input-conditioned memory from persistent updates, or explain how optimizer updates interact with EWMA and gradient detachment across batches. Since tokens are pooled across images, these choices determine whether predictions depend on other evaluation images or previous batches. The asserted insensitivity to batch size lacks quantitative supporting results.

The efficiency claims are broader than the measurements support. AiT retains dense self-attention and computes attention scores over the complete token pool before top-k selection. Table 1 supports a favorable depth–accuracy tradeoff against ViT, but AiT-Small is substantially larger than Coordination: 15.8M versus 2.2M parameters. Figure 3 provides a favorable single-block comparison; full-model comparisons at matched budgets and measurements of runtime or memory are missing. General computational superiority over sparse Transformers is therefore not established.

The baseline comparisons leave uncertainty about practical generality. Luna reaches only 47.86% on CIFAR-10, and Figure 2 shows ViT-Base deteriorating substantially after approximately 50 epochs. The manuscript does not provide a validation/checkpoint-selection protocol or detailed baseline tuning results that explain these outcomes. The reported improvements remain meaningful, but stronger support is needed for claims that competing architectures inherently fail to scale.

Secondary reproducibility issues include conflicting learning rates in Section 4.1 and Table 8 (10⁻⁵ versus 10⁻⁴), an unspecified ImageNet100 class subset, and incomplete dataset split details. Code availability is promised rather than supplied in the manuscript. strengths: The Global Workspace Layer provides a coherent, potentially useful combination of low-dimensional persistent memory, sparse token selection, and associative retrieval. Its modular design makes the contribution relevant to vision Transformer architectures. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-9nteyno6/call-af7105d56a5544dca3d951197601a48f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The ViT comparisons demonstrate meaningful gains under the reported training conditions. In Table 1, AiT-Medium achieves 84.59%/60.58% on CIFAR-10/100 versus ViT-Base's 83.82%/57.92%, using 45.9M versus 85.7M parameters and approximately half the reported FLOPs.
The relational reasoning results provide evidence beyond image classification: Table 6 reports 80.03% relational accuracy for AiT-Base, compared with 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base.

Table 3 systematically examines the memory, retrieval, balancing loss, bottleneck, and self-attention components. Reported variation across three runs, initialization experiments, and temperature sensitivity analysis strengthen the empirical investigation.
weaknesses: The selected-instance loss has a consequential technical problem as written. Equation 3 uses A defined as dense softmax attention, whose entries are positive; therefore every token's load equals M and the load-variance term is zero. If A instead denotes masked top-k attention, the hard indicator supplies no gradient through ordinary backpropagation, and no differentiable estimator is specified. The importance term can still train, but the claimed contribution of the load term is unsupported.

The evaluation memory protocol is unresolved. Section 3.2 states that explicit memory is frozen during evaluation, yet Appendix F/Table 9 reports changes when its writing attention is disabled. Algorithm 1 does not distinguish frozen parameters, temporary batch-conditioned memory, and persistent state updates. Because writing pools tokens across images, this ambiguity affects whether predictions depend on other test samples or their ordering, making the evaluation difficult to reproduce and interpret.

The Hopfield contribution is insufficiently isolated. For the cited modern Hopfield energy, one update is mathematically attention with tied keys and values. Replacing it with fully parameterized multi-head cross-attention changes parameterization and computation, so the ablation does not isolate a benefit from energy-based dynamics. Moreover, one update generally does not attain the argmin in Equation 6; the claim that all tokens reach their minima is stronger than the demonstrated energy reduction.

The broader superiority claims exceed the comparisons. Table 6 omits the Relation Network from the original Sort-of-CLEVR work and specialized reasoning approaches discussed in the introduction. ImageNet100 compares only against ViT. These experiments support gains over the listed implementations, but provide limited evidence for the claimed state-of-the-art positioning or for prior specialization being the cause of improved reasoning.

Practical efficiency remains only partly established. AiT retains dense self-attention and computes dense memory-to-token scores before top-k selection. The reported parameter and FLOP savings from reducing depth are valuable, but there are no runtime, peak-memory, or sequence-length scaling measurements supporting the broader training-efficiency claims.

Additional reproducibility gaps include conflicting learning rates in Section 4.1 and Table 8 (1e-5 versus 1e-4), an unspecified ImageNet100 class subset, and no clear validation protocol for hyperparameter selection. These reporting issues are correctable; the unresolved loss, inference protocol, and retrieval attribution are the material concerns that outweigh the supported empirical gains and determine my weak reject recommendation.
